steps.observation: You have 10 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The last storm took the sound of the sea with it.

Elias noticed three days after the waves had calmed. He woke, dressed by habit, lit the lamp, checked the oil, polished the glass—everything as he had done for thirty-two years. Only when he stepped onto the gallery and looked down did he realize something was missing.

The surf rolled and broke against the black teeth of rock far below, but in utter silence, like a play performed behind thick glass. He pressed his hands to his ears, thinking of age, of illness, but the creak of the railing and his own sharp breath reached him clearly. Only the sea was mute.

He sent a message to the mainland by radio. No reply came. The set hummed faintly; the needles quivered, alive but unhelpful. The supply boat that usually cut a white wake toward him every Thursday never appeared. Days stacked like stones.

At night the lamp still swung its slow revolutions, a white pulse against a deaf world. Ships passed, distant constellations of navigation lights gliding along the horizon, but none veered close. None signaled. Once, a great red hull drifted nearer than was safe. Elias rang the fog bell out of reflex, and the hammer struck metal with a dull, private note that did not travel. The ship slid by unharmed, guided by something other than sound or sight.

On the seventeenth silent dawn, he saw a girl standing on the low tide shelf, where no one should have been able to stand. Her dress blew about her legs, but the fabric made no whisper. She looked up at the lighthouse and raised a hand.

He climbed down the winding iron steps, each footfall echoing in the stone throat of the tower, and stepped out to meet her. The air smelled of salt and wet iron, but the sea itself lay like a painting—waves arching, foam suspended, never quite arriving.

“You’re still lighting it,” she said. Her voice was thin but audible, as if carried from very far away.

“That’s my work,” Elias answered. “There are ships.”

“Not anymore.” She touched the water’s edge with her bare toes. The wave that should have soaked her remained arched, inches from her skin. “You’re late,” she added.

“For what?”

“For letting go.” She pointed past him, to the lighthouse. The stone was brighter than it should have been in dawn’s gray, edges too sharp, as if freshly drawn. “The storm took more than you think.”

Elias’s memory caught like a net on something heavy: a wall of black water, the lamp going out, his hands slick on the wheel of the backup generator, the sudden crash and then—nothing. No pain. No darkness. Only the next morning, getting up as he always did.

“Am I dead?” he asked.

The girl tilted her head. “The sea keeps what it can. Some things wash back slowly.”

The realization did not hurt. It settled over him like a coat that had always been his size.

“And the light?” he said. “The ships?”

She smiled, but there was sadness in it. “There are no ships left to save. They have other lights now, in places you won’t go. You’re keeping watch over an empty horizon.”

They stood in the not-quite-surf, listening to a sea that refused to speak.

“Then why am I still here?” Elias asked.

“Because you believe the light must never go out,” the girl said. “And because lighthouses are stubborn things. They stay even when the maps forget them.”

He looked up at his tower. In its revolving eye, he saw himself as he had been at twenty, at forty, at sixty: trimming the wick, checking his logbook, marking storms and ships and the long blue pauses between. The thought of going back up and doing it again made him feel both weary and oddly comforted.

“What happens,” he said, “if I let it go dark?”

For the first time since the storm, the sea moved. The wave completed its fall, hissing over the stones. Sound returned in a single breathless roar that made his eyes sting. Above, gulls shrieked. The wind found its voice. It was like surfacing after a long, unintended dive.

“Then the sea can remember itself,” the girl said.

He hesitated, fingers flexing at his sides, feeling phantom weight: the key ring, the lantern, the oil can. “Will there be anyone to guide?” His own voice shook.

She shrugged. “Maybe not. Maybe that’s no longer your work.”

He thought of all the nights when a flicker on the black water had straightened his spine with purpose, each time a horn answered his beam with a blast of gratitude. The logs stacked in his desk upstairs, the careful script: 2:15 a.m., ship to the east, four blasts; 3:47 a.m., light rain, visibility poor.

“It’s all I know,” he whispered.

“Then let me keep it,” the girl said softly. “You can go.”

Elias looked at her closely. Her eyes reflected the lantern’s absent glow, though the sun was already climbing. “Who are you?”

“Someone who needs a light,” she said. “For a little while longer.”

He thought of refusing. Of clinging to the tower, to his routine. But the sea was speaking again, and its voice was not asking; it was inviting.

“Mind the lens,” he said at last. “Dust makes shadows where you don’t want them.”

Her smile widened. “I will.”

He turned away from the lighthouse and walked toward the water. It rose to meet him, cool around his ankles, knees, chest, the roar of it in his ears like all the storms he had ever known, braided into a single, immense sound. He did not look back.

Behind him, the lamp flared to life one last time under a smaller, steady hand. The beam swept the brightening horizon, not because someone was coming, but because someone was going, and needed to see the way out.

When the sun climbed fully and washed the sea with gold, the old lighthouse on the forgotten rock still turned its patient eye, no longer a warning, but a farewell.
